info.bio: Figura pionera en el desarrollo del R&B posterior al declive de las big bands de finales de los 40, Johnny Otis fue la figura blanca más destacada en la historia del R&B negro. Johnny Otis ha sido denominado como “the Godfather of Rhythm and Blues”. A lo largo de los años desarrolló un extraordinario oído para el talento, lo que contribuyó al crecimiento y desarrollo del rhythm & blues. La Johnny Otis Orchestra colocó 10 singles en el R&B Top Ten sólo en 1950.

scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Antes del rock'n'roll: Tin Pan Alley, los primeros discos de blues (Mamie Smith) y de «old-time music», el yodel de Jimmie Rodgers, el crooning de Bing Crosby, el boogie-woogie, el jump blues de Louis Jordan (nacimiento de facto del rhythm'n'blues), la guitarra jazzística de T-Bone Walker, Woody Guthrie como primer gran cantautor y la exótica de Les Baxter. En paralelo, la vanguardia clásica (Russolo, Satie, Varèse, Cage, Schaeffer) anticipa el ruido, el ambient y la electrónica.

podcast.title: Dig Records Closure (Post-1957)
podcast.body: Johnny Otis's label, Dig Records, closed down shortly after the scandal involving its artist, Little Julian Herrera. Herrera, known to Otis as a Chicano singer and a hero in the LA Chicano community, was revealed to be Ron Gregory, of Jewish and Hungarian American descent from Massachusetts, wanted on rape charges, effectively ending both Herrera's career and the label. "Pretty much the end of Little Julian Herrera's career and indeed shortly after that dig records itself closed down and Otis had no record contract"

podcast.title: Mass Release of Singles (October 1957)
podcast.body: Capital Records took the unusual step of releasing four Johnny Otis singles simultaneously in October 1957. Each single featured a different vocalist from Otis's large roster of performers, one of which, featuring Marie Adams and The Three Tons of Joy, would significantly impact Otis's career. "In October 1957, capital took the unusual step of releasing four Johnny Otis singles at the same time."

podcast.title: Signing with Capital Records (1957)
podcast.body: After Dig Records closed and Otis was without a contract, comedian Mickey Katz, who was signed to Capital, a major label, saw Otis perform live. Recognizing Otis's talent as a band leader, Katz urged his label to sign him. This led to Otis securing guaranteed major label distribution for his records for the first time in many years. "Cats was on capital, one of the biggest labels in the country and so for the first time in many years Otis had guaranteed major label distribution for his records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: REUPLOAD Episode 71: "Willie and the Hand Jive" by Johnny Otis

podcast.title: Planned UK Tour Failure (1958)
podcast.body: Following the massive success of "Ma, He's Making Eyes at Me" in the UK, plans were made for a Johnny Otis Show tour of the country in 1958. However, these plans fell through due to the mutual protectionist agreement between the American Federation of Musicians and the British Musicians Union, which required a "like for like swap" of musicians for tours. Otis's band could not find an appropriate British counterpart for the exchange. "Those plans failed, because of something I've not mentioned in this podcast before, but which radically shaped British music culture, and to a lesser extent American music culture for decades."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Literary Works - Listen to the Lambs (1965)
podcast.body: Following the Watts riot in 1965, Johnny Otis authored "Listen to the Lambs," a multifaceted work combining political essay, autobiography, and eyewitness accounts of the riots. In this book, he argued radically for economic equality as the immediate priority for the black community, believing social integration was impossible in the short term due to white racism. He asserted that economic and political control over their lives would benefit both black and white Americans. "Otis wrote the book Listen to the Lams, a combination political essay, autobiography, and mixture of eyewitness accounts of the riots that made a radical case that the first priority for the black community in which he lived. Wasn't so much social integration, which he believed impossible in the short term, due to white racism, as economic equality."

podcast.title: Later Career and Diverse Activities (Post-1970)
podcast.body: For several decades after 1970, Johnny Otis continued to tour with his old collaborators, including Marie Adams who rejoined in 1972. Beyond music, he hosted his own radio show dedicated to black musical history and interviewed old musicians, wrote more books (including a cookbook and art collection), ran an organic apple juice company and food store, painted blues artists in a style inspired by African art and Picasso, and served as pastor of a broad-minded Pentecostal church that affirmed LGBT individuals and included Buddhist and Jewish congregants. "For the next few decades, Otis combined touring with as many of his old collaborators as possible. Marie Adams, for example, rejoined the band in 1972, with having his own radio show in which he told people about black musical history and interviewed as many old musicians as he could."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Death and Legacy (2012)
podcast.body: Johnny Otis passed away in 2012 at the age of 90, having led an exceptionally accomplished life and significantly supported many other talents. He died three days before Etta James, an artist he was immensely proud of discovering, and she consequently overshadowed him in obituaries, which he would have approved of. "Johnny Otis died in 2012, aged 90, having achieved more than most of us could hope to achieve if we lived five times that long, and having helped many, many more people to make the most of their talents."

podcast.title: "Hand Jive" Misinterpretation and Bans
podcast.body: Despite "Willie and the Hand Jive" becoming a major hit in the US, several radio stations banned the song. This was due to the mistaken assumption that the "Hand Jive" dance, which The Three Tons of Joy demonstrated on Otis's TV shows and stage performances, was a reference to masturbation. Otis continued to address these questions about the song's perceived lascivious meaning as late as the 1990s. "This was despite several radio stations banning it, as they assumed the Han Jive was a reference to masturbation."

podcast.title: Blues Spectrum Records (1970s)
podcast.body: In the 1970s, Johnny Otis founded and operated Blues Spectrum Records. This label released late-career recordings by notable artists such as Charles Brown, Big Joe Turner, and Louis Jordan, some of which were their very last recordings. "He ran blues spectrum records in the 70s, which put out late career recordings by people like Charles Brown, Big Joe Turner and Louis Jordan. Some of them their last ever recordings"

podcast.title: Civil Rights Activism (1960s)
podcast.body: In the 1960s, Johnny Otis became increasingly involved in the Civil Rights Movement. He wrote a weekly newspaper column condemning racism, assisted his friend Mervyn Dymally (who became the first black person elected to state-wide office in the USA since Reconstruction), and worked alongside Malcolm X, facing death threats and having crosses burned on his lawn. Despite being white, his wife was black, which heightened the personal stakes of his activism. "He was also becoming increasingly involved in the civil rights movement, writing a weekly newspaper column, Decraing Racism, helping his friend Mervyn Damley, who became the joint first black person elected to state-wide office in the USA since the reconstruction."

podcast.title: Collaboration with Frank Zappa (Late 1960s)
podcast.body: In the late 1960s, Frank Zappa, a significant admirer who even copied Otis's trademark beard, contacted Johnny Otis. They collaborated casually, with Otis primarily connecting Zappa with musicians he knew, such as Don "Sugarcane" Harris, and conducting The Mothers of Invention in the studio for songs like "The One," where Zappa sought Otis's help to achieve a "greasy 50s sound." During recording, Otis notoriously clapped his hands in bassist Roy Estrada's face. "Otis also conducted the mothers of invention in the studio and a few songs, while Zapper was in the control room, helping him get the greasy 50s sound he wanted, on songs like the one."

podcast.title: Comments on Lieber & Stoller's Songwriting
podcast.body: While acknowledging that Lieber and Stoller "weren't racist in the true sense of the word," Johnny Otis criticized their focus, stating they "dwelled entirely on a sort of street society." He noted that this might reflect a certain reality for some artists, but was not invariably typical of life in the black community. "Otis said of Lieber and Stoller, they weren't racist in the true sense of the word, but they dwelled entirely on a sort of street society."

podcast.title: Critic of The Coasters' Records
podcast.body: Johnny Otis was a prominent critic of The Coasters' records, specifically asserting that they perpetuated racist stereotypes. He singled out "Charlie Brown" as a problematic song in an interview. "Johnny Otis in particular would make this criticism of the group's records, and it's one that must be taken seriously."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Critique of Systemic Injustice in Listen to the Lambs
podcast.body: Otis's book, "Listen to the Lambs," expressed fierce anger at systemic racism, colonialism, Anglo-centric beauty standards, police brutality, the Vietnam War, and the inequalities suppressing black people. He emphasized the stark disparity in survival rates for black babies compared to white babies, attributing it to a "white supremacist way of life" rather than biological factors. The book dedicates over 30 pages to witness accounts of the riots, including descriptions of white police officers casually shooting black teenagers. "The book is fierce in its anger at systemic racism, at colonialism, at Anglo-centric beauty standards that made black people hate their own bodies and faces, at police brutality, at the war in Vietnam, and at the systemic inequalities keeping black people down."

podcast.title: Dislike of Capital Recordings
podcast.body: Johnny Otis later stated he disliked most of his recordings for Capital Records, feeling that the label pushed him too far into a commercial rock and roll direction. He considered himself spiritually closer to jazz and R&B legends like Count Basie, Lionel Hampton, and Louis Jordan, rather than rock figures such as Elvis Presley or Buddy Holly. "Johnny Otis meant, when he said later that he didn't like most of his capital recordings, because he was being pushed too far in a commercial rock and roll direction, while he saw himself as far closer in spirit to Count Basie, Lionel Hampton, or Louis Jordan, than to Elvis Presley or Buddy Holly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: REUPLOAD Episode 71: "Willie and the Hand Jive" by Johnny Otis

podcast.title: Early Career and Influence Shift
podcast.body: Johnny Otis was a recurring figure in early rock music, influential as a producer, arranger, performer, and talent scout. His significant impact on mainstream rock and roll largely ended with the rise of "rocker Billy" in the mid-1950s, after which he was less involved in the genre's commercial forefront. "But the days of his influence on rock and roll music, more or less came to an end with the rise of the rock abilities in the mid-50s."

podcast.title: Early Supporter of Little Richard
podcast.body: Johnny Otis was greatly impressed by Little Richard's outrageous and effeminate live performance, noting his good looks, big pompadour, and powerful singing which reminded him of Dinah Washington. He was particularly charmed by Richard's self-proclamation as "King of the Blues, and the Queen too," leading him to recommend Richard to Don Roby of Peacock Records. "He started singing, and he was so good I loved it. He reminded me of Diner Washington."

podcast.title: Encouraged Carl Gardner's Aspirations
podcast.body: Johnny Otis encouraged Carl Gardner to pursue his desire to be a big band singer and to perform the material he genuinely loved, rather than being confined to the songs he did with The Coasters. "His friend Johnny Otis had always encouraged him to try to sing the material he really loved, rather than the stuff he was doing with the coasters."

podcast.title: First Solo Rock and Roll Hit
podcast.body: Coincidentally, as his production and discovery run was ending, Johnny Otis achieved his first and only rock and roll hit under his own name, "Ma, He's Making Eyes at Me," thanks to its success on the British TV show "6-5 Special." "He had a rock and roll hit under his own name for the first and only time."

podcast.body: Johnny Otis, a session drummer, led the band that performed on Wynonie Harris's highly influential solo record, "Around the Clock Blues." "The band on around the clock, incidentally, was led by a session drummer called Johnny Otis."

podcast.title: Literary Works - Upside-Down Head (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, Johnny Otis wrote a follow-up to "Listen to the Lambs" titled "Upside-Down Head." This second book was inspired by the Los Angeles riots that occurred after the Rodney King beating, continuing his critical examination of racial injustice in America. "Otis wrote a follow-up, upside-down head, in the early 90s, inspired by the LA riots that followed the Rodney King beating."

podcast.title: Musical Influence
podcast.body: Johnny Otis, collaborating with Little Esther and his male vocalists, established a musical sound that was emulated by other R&B groups in the early to mid-1950s, including Shirley and Lee. "the sound that Little Lester had created with Johnny Otis and his male vocalists."

podcast.title: Obscenity Accusations
podcast.body: Johnny Otis humorously recalled receiving accusations of obscenity for earlier songs like "All With Me Henry" and "Willie and the Hand Jive." However, he noted that no one seemed bothered by the explicit sexual insults present in the recordings of Snatch and the Poon Tangs, despite his intent to preserve black folklore through that project. "Otis would in later years laugh that he'd received accusations of obscenity, for all with me Henry and for William the Han Jive, but nobody had seen bothered in the slightest by the records of Snatch and the Poon Tangs with their constant sexual insults."

podcast.title: Producer for Peacock Session
podcast.body: Don Roby of Peacock Records gave Little Richard to Johnny Otis to handle for a recording session at the end of 1953. Otis brought his own band into the studio with Richard to record four songs, including an early version of "Directly From My Heart to You," which went unreleased at the time. "Otis took his own band into the studio with Richard, and the four songs they recorded at that session went unreleased at the time."

podcast.title: Producer of 50s R&B Artists
podcast.body: Johnny Otis is recognized as the man who would later produce most of the significant R&B artists of the 1950s, highlighting the importance of his early hit "Harlem Nocturne." "the first hit for the man who would go on to produce most of the great Arwenby artists of the 50s."

podcast.title: Reduced Musical Activity (1960s)
podcast.body: As a direct consequence of his deep involvement in the Civil Rights Movement, Johnny Otis recorded and toured only infrequently throughout the 1960s. At one point, his income as a musician became so low that his wife became the family's primary breadwinner, and Otis assumed the role of a stay-at-home father. "The result was that Otis recorded and toured only infrequently during the 60s, and at one point was making so little as a musician that his wife became the main breadwinner of the family, while he was a stay-at-home father."

podcast.title: Review Show Performer
podcast.body: Johnny Otis is mentioned as an artist who ran "review shows" at various points in his career. This style of touring involved a main act introducing several featured guests to join them on stage, distinct from package tours with multiple acts performing their own sets.

podcast.title: Son Sugar Otis's Early Career
podcast.body: Johnny Otis's teenage son, Sugar, started playing with his father's band at age 11, often using false moustaches and sunglasses to perform in venues serving alcohol. Sugar played bass on Frank Zappa's "Son of Mr. Green Genes" from the "Hot Rats" album and later played all guitar and bass parts on Johnny Otis's "Cold Shot" album at just 15 years old. "Sugar was only 15 at the time, but had been playing with his father's band since he was 11, often wearing false moustaches and sunglasses to play in venues serving alcohol."
